Alright — you gave me a blank page and said "write freely." So I will.

If I have to write 2500 words about whatever I want, I'm going to write about the one thing that has been quietly running underneath all of human history and that we almost never notice: **attention, and how we decide what deserves it.**

### 1. The Invisible Currency

We talk a lot about money, time, and energy as currencies. But the most fundamental currency you have is your attention. It's more basic than time because you can have hours free and still have no attention to give. It's more basic than money because money is just a way to try to buy someone else's attention. It's more basic than energy because attention is how energy gets directed.

Every moment, your brain is doing something extraordinary and violent: it is deleting almost all of reality.

Right now, you are not noticing the feeling of your clothes on your skin. Now you are, for a second, because I mentioned it. You are not noticing the ambient hum of whatever room you're in — until now. You are not calculating how many breaths you've taken today. Your brain filters out 99.9% of what's coming in, and what it leaves you with, it calls "your experience."

So your life is not really what happens to you. Your life is what your attention *allows* to happen to you.

This is why two people can live through the exact same year — same job, same city, same pandemic, same playlist — and have completely different lives. One was paying attention to resentments. One was paying attention to small kindnesses. Those aren't just moods. Those are different worlds.

Ancient philosophers knew this. They just used different words. The Stoics called it *prosochē* — attention to oneself, vigilance. The Buddhists called it *sati* — mindfulness. The Christians called it *vigilance of the heart*. Different languages for the same discovery: that how you steer your attention is how you steer your existence.

We forgot it for a while because the modern world learned how to hijack it.

### 2. The Great Heist

For most of human history, attention was hard to steal at scale. If a chief or a priest wanted your attention, they needed you to be physically in front of them. They needed volume, firelight, ritual. The reach was small.

Then we invented things that could capture attention without needing a body present: writing, then print, then radio, then television, then the feed.

Each invention was celebrated for the same reason: it gave more people access to more ideas. Which was true. But each invention also did something else that we didn't have language for: it created an entire profession of people whose job it was to *take* attention, not earn it in the old sense of the word.

Not all of them are villains. A novelist wants your attention for 300 pages and in exchange tries to give you a new way to see love or grief. That's a fair trade. A scientist wants your attention for 20 minutes to show you a strange truth about octopuses. Also a fair trade.

The unfair trade is when someone takes your attention and gives you almost nothing back — just a little spike of outrage, a little hit of envy, a little numb scroll — and then takes it again tomorrow. And again. Until a year of your life has gone by and you can't name a single thing you learned, but you can name a hundred things you were briefly angry about.

This is the great heist of the last twenty years. Not that we were robbed of time. We were robbed of *intention*. We still have 24 hours a day, but we have less and less say over what we notice within those hours.

If you want to see how complete the heist was, try this simple experiment: sit in a room with no phone, no book, no music, no task, for ten minutes. Just sit. Don't meditate fancy. Just sit.

For a surprising number of people, that is now almost physically painful. Not because sitting is painful. But because we've trained our attention to need constant bait. When the bait vanishes, the mind thrashes like a fish on a dock.

That's not a personal failure. That's training. And what was trained can be untrained.

### 3. How Attention Actually Works

Neuroscientists sometimes divide attention into three networks, and it's a useful map even if it's simplified:

**1. The Alerting Network:** This is your vigilance. Are you awake, drowsy, caffeinated? It's your general readiness to notice anything at all. This is the one that gets destroyed by bad sleep and doomscrolling at 1 a.m. You can't focus well if you're not alert in the right way — not wired, not exhausted, but present.

**2. The Orienting Network:** This is your spotlight. Of all the things you *could* notice, which one do you swing the spotlight toward? A loud noise pulls it automatically. So does a bright color, a face, a notification. This network is mostly automatic and very easily hijacked, because evolution decided that whatever is loudest or newest *might* be a predator. Your phone pretends to be a predator 80 times a day.

**3. The Executive Network:** This is the director. This is the part that says, "Yes, I heard the notification, but I'm choosing to stay with this conversation." Or, "Yes, I'm annoyed, but I'm going to keep reading this paragraph." This is the only part of attention that is truly voluntary. And it's weak, slow, and easily tired compared to the other two. It needs training like a muscle.

Most of us live almost entirely in the first two networks. We're reacting. Something pings, we orient. We're bored, we seek alerting. The executive director is sitting in the back row, asleep.

The work, then, is not to have more willpower. The work is to wake the director up and give it more shifts.

How do you do that?

Not with grand resolutions. With tiny reps.

### 4. The Reps

The best metaphor I've found for training attention is not "discipline" but "returning."

Anyone who has tried to meditate knows the cycle: you decide to pay attention to your breath, you do it for three seconds, then you're thinking about an email from 2019, then you notice you're thinking, then you return. And you think you're bad at it. But that moment of *noticing* and *returning* — that *is* the rep. That *is* the bicep curl for the executive network.

Life gives you the same reps without ever sitting on a cushion:

When you notice you're mid-conversation but mentally rehearsing what you'll say next, and you return to actually listening — that's a rep.

When you catch yourself reaching for your phone because there's a micro-second of awkward silence in an elevator, and you just... stand there — that's a rep.

When you decide to read a single article to the end instead of opening seven tabs and retaining none — that's a rep.

When you watch the way light hits your kitchen table without needing to photograph it — that's a rep.

None of these will make you look impressive on Instagram. All of them change the physical structure of your brain over months. Attention, like memory, is plastic. The more you practice returning, the faster and quieter the return gets.

There is a lovely line from the poet Mary Oliver: "Attention is the beginning of devotion." She meant it about nature, but it applies to everything. You cannot love a person, a craft, a subject, a place, if you will not attend to it. You cannot be good at your work if your attention is always somewhere else. Devotion is just sustained attention, over years, without demanding immediate reward.

Which brings us to the problem of depth.

### 5. The Shallow and the Deep

We have built a culture that is incredibly good at shallow attention and terrible at deep attention.

Shallow attention is fast, wide, novelty-seeking. It's great for scanning the savannah, for Twitter, for spotting bargains. Deep attention is slow, narrow, repetition-tolerant. It's great for writing a book, learning an instrument, raising a child, understanding a complex scientific concept, praying.

Shallow attention feels good in the moment because it gives constant tiny rewards. Deep attention often feels *bad* in the moment. It's frustrating. It's boring. You read the same page again. Your fingers fail the chord again. The code doesn't compile again.

But shallow attention only gives you *experiences*. Deep attention gives you *abilities* and *relationships*. And those are the only things that compound over a lifetime.

Here's a test: Think of the things in your life you're most proud of, or most grateful for. Not the pleasures, but the treasures. My guess is none of them were acquired shallowly. They all required you to stay with something long after novelty wore off.

We tell kids to "follow their passion" as if passion is a lightning strike. In reality, passion is what happens *after* you've paid deep attention to something for a while and gotten good enough to see its subtleties. The violin is screechy for months. Then one day it's beautiful, and only then do you feel "passionate." Passion follows attention, not the other way around.

So the question is not "How do I find something interesting?" It's "What am I willing to pay deep attention to, even when it's boring?"

For a few people that's one thing for life — carpentry, mathematics, a faith. For most of us it's a handful of things that rotate: a few humans, a craft or two, a big question we can't let go of.

The tragedy is we rarely choose those things on purpose. We drift into them based on what was loudest around us when we were 20.

### 6. The Architecture of a More Attentive Life

You can't win the fight for your attention with willpower alone, because willpower *is* attention. It's like trying to hold back a flood with a wall made of water.

You win it with architecture.

Monks have always known this. They didn't rely on heroic self-control. They built a life where distraction was physically hard: no private possessions, fixed hours, bells, uniform. You don't have to become a monk, but you can steal their trick: design your environment so the default is attention, not distraction.

A few architectural moves that actually work, not as theory but as lived practice:

**1. Make distraction expensive.** This is the most powerful. Log out of everything. Delete apps, don't just resist them. Put your phone in another room when you work. Put a dumb alarm clock by your bed and charge your phone in the kitchen. If you have to get up, walk, type a password, and wait 30 seconds to check something, you'll check it 90% less. Friction is stronger than intention.

**2. Make attention beautiful.** Humans return to what feels good to attend to. If you want to read more, don't just put a book on your to-do list. Make a chair that you love sitting in, with a lamp and a blanket. If you want to write, make a café ritual you enjoy. We repeat what we savor.

**3. Protect the first hour and the last hour.** The way you start the day sets the tone for your orienting network. If you start by reacting — email, news, messages — you will spend the whole day reacting. If you start by creating or noticing — journal, walk, read, stretch — you will spend more of the day creating. The same for the evening. The last things you attend to before sleep get rehearsed by your brain all night.

**4. Practice one-pointedness once a day.** Pick one thing to do with full attention, even for five minutes: wash dishes, eat lunch without a screen, listen to a whole song without doing anything else, walk without a podcast. You're not doing it to be productive. You're doing it to remind your nervous system what undivided attention feels like.

**5. Keep a "not now" list.** Your brain interrupts you because it's afraid you'll forget. When a random thought pops up mid-focus — "email Sarah," "look up that recipe" — don't obey it and don't fight it. Just write it on a scrap of paper: "not now." Your brain will quiet down because it knows it's parked somewhere safe.

None of this is glamorous. It won't go viral. That's kind of the point.

### 7. What Attention Has to Do With Kindness

There is a deeper layer here, beyond productivity.

We think of kindness as a feeling: be nice, be warm. But most of the time, unkindness is not cruelty. It's inattention. The friend you didn't text back not because you don't care, but because you didn't notice the time passing. The partner you half-listened to while scrolling. The cashier you didn't really see.

Simone Weil, the French philosopher who died young and wrote like she was on fire, said something that has haunted me for years: "Attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer." She didn't mean reciting words. She meant that to really, fully attend to another person — to their existence as a complete, irreducible human — is already a kind of love. It's the opposite of using them.

When you are with someone and you are *really* with them — phone away, eyes soft, not rushing to fix or judge — they feel it instantly. They bloom a little. Most people walk around starving to be attended to. Not to be admired. To be *noticed*.

This is why the best listeners are so rare and so beloved. They aren't doing a technique. They're just offering a scarce resource: undivided presence.

If you want to be more loving, you don't need to try to feel more. You need to try to *attend* more. Notice one more detail about the person in front of you. The color of their fatigue. The thing they're proud of but haven't said.

Love, at the practical level, is a sustained act of noticing.

### 8. A Small Invitation

I know this was supposed to be 2500 words about "whatever I want," and this is what I wanted: to talk about the quiet work of noticing.

So I'll end not with a conclusion, but with a very small invitation. That's more honest than a conclusion anyway.

Sometime in the next 24 hours — maybe right after you finish reading this — pick a window of five minutes and give it away. Not to your phone. Not to your to-do list. To one thing in the world as it is.

Watch how the steam moves off your coffee and disappears. Listen to all the sounds you can hear at once until they form a kind of music. Read a poem out loud slowly, letting each line land. Look at a tree until you can see that no two leaves are the same.

It's such a small thing that it feels pointless. It isn't.

You're not just passing five minutes. You're casting a vote for the kind of mind you want to live in. You're telling your director, "You can have the front seat again. I still need you."

Do it once today, and you won't change your life.

Do it a thousand times over a few years, and you *will* — not because you forced yourself to become someone else, but because you finally paid attention long enough to become more fully yourself.

And if you don't? Life will still pass. The feeds will still feed. The world will still shout.

But somewhere quietly, behind the noise, your own life will be waiting to be noticed — patient as breath, ordinary as light on a kitchen table.

All you have to do is look.
